extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of Old English literature, translators and textual critics working on Beowulf
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly notes and guidance for editing and translating Old English poetry (Beowulf): how to read the manuscript, propose emendations, justify lexical/syntactic choices, and render lines into idiomatic modern English. Intended to guide critical editions and translators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer attested secondary meanings before emending
rubrics_metrics.description: When a manuscript word 'baffles' (appears anomalous) prefer to see if it has an attested secondary meaning in the literature rather than emend immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the MS 'under' in two passages is treated in a secondary sense 'in' (cf. Chron. 876, March's A.-S. Gram. §355, Oro. Amaz. I.10) instead of emending to a different preposition. The note cites parallels in Old English and a modern English idiom ('in such circumstances' ~ 'under such circumstances') to justify keeping the manuscript reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallels in other texts and grammars to justify readings and senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Support translation and sense decisions by citing occurrences of the same word or idiom in other Old English/Teutonic texts or grammars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cite Chron. 876 and Oro. Amaz. I.10 and March's Anglo-Saxon Grammar §355 to justify meanings; compare idiomatic uses across Old English and Old Saxon and other Teutonic languages to interpret constructions like the accusative + þæt-clause with geweorðan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose emendations when manuscript reading is implausible, but give rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When the manuscript text yields an implausible or unintelligible reading, propose specific emendations and explain why they are preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: B. suggests emending to 'under hróf genam' (v.1303) or emending compounds like néod-laðu → néad-láðum. The editor lists alternative readings offered by other editors (K., t.B., Kl., Sw., R.) and explains linguistic or contextual reasons for preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze compound morphology before deciding meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine morphological structure of compounds (elements, inflections) to determine whether to accept MS form or reconstruct a variant, and translate accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discussion of 'néod-laðu' vs suggested 'néad-láðum' with an offered translation ('asked whether the night had been pleasant to him after crushing-hostility'). Editor assesses morphological plausibility and renders the gloss consistent with the reconstructed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render both literal and idiomatic translations, and justify choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a literal, close translation alongside a freer idiomatic rendering when helpful, and explain which sense is intended and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: passage (v.1599–1600) is translated literally ('Then many agreed upon this (namely), that the sea-wolf had killed him.') with discussion of the underlying idiom; elsewhere literal glosses are contrasted with smoother English renderings and the translator comments which reading preserves the original force best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept attested grammatical anomalies when evidenced by parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not forcibly 'correct' grammatical oddities (e.g., gender disagreement) if the construction is attested elsewhere; note and cite parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Sé Þe' (1345) is a masculine relative referring to a feminine antecedent; the note cites v.1888 as another instance. The editor records such anomalies as legitimate attestations rather than errors to be regularized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emend tense or form to harmonize narrative when justified by context
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust verb tense or other forms to bring passages into consistent narrative tense when the MS reading produces awkward or discordant tense usage, provided contextual evidence supports the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: changing 'is' to 'wæs' (v.2025) is suggested to harmonize tenses in a passage (v.2025–2027); the editor explains how the emendation yields better temporal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss variant readings and cite scholarly opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: List alternate readings from different editors/scholars for disputed words or lines, and state the editor's preferred reading with reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous footnotes enumerate variants (K., t.B., Kl., Sw., R., Gr., etc.), e.g., 'gefrægnod' vs 'gefægnod', 'hrímge' vs 'hrínde', 'feaxe' vs 'eaxle', 'cyning-balde' vs 'cyning-holde'; the editor records each variant, translates consequences, and gives the rationale for choosing one over another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gloss obscure words and offer semantic identifications/cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify obscure or disputed lexical items, propose meanings (sometimes with probable etymology), and cross-reference similar usages or glosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'bróden-mæl' is interpreted as probably 'damaskeened sword'; 'hrímge' vs 'hrínde' with translations; explanatory notes cite other passages and lexicons to support these identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain idiomatic and syntactic constructions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a construction is unusual (idiom, syntax), explain its structure and sense, showing how the elements fit together so a correct translation follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the idiom with the impersonal verb 'geweorðan' used with an accusative of person and a þæt-clause meaning 'agree' is explained with multiple Old English and Orosius citations; the editor then translates problematic passages using that syntactic understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the sense and register of the original over word-for-word literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to render the original meaning and poetic effect rather than slavishly translating each word if doing so would obscure sense or idiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening note states 'The sense of the translation would be the same.' Throughout the notes the translator prefers readings and renderings that keep the original semantic force (e.g., rendering 'æse wlanc' in parallel with suggested translations) and occasionally smooths idiomatic English while flagging literal alternatives.
